front: A mass on a spring has period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$, so its period is independent of {{c1::amplitude and gravity}}.
why: Spring period equation and its amplitude independence; calculated every year

front: A simple pendulum has period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$, so its period is independent of {{c1::the bob's mass}}.
why: Pendulum period equation and mass independence; tested every year

front: A sound wave passes from air into soft tissue. Which wave properties change?
why: Frequency fixed across media; restated by the shorter constant-frequency card

front: Contrast longitudinal and transverse waves.
why: Longitudinal vs transverse waves; foundational wave definition

front: In simple harmonic motion, where are speed and acceleration each maximal?
why: SHM speed max at equilibrium, acceleration max at extremes; common discrete

front: Leg swing during walking behaves like a pendulum, so a taller person's natural cadence is {{c1::slower}}.
why: Walking cadence pendulum analogy is trivia

front: Relate wave speed, frequency, and wavelength.
why: v=f*lambda; foundational wave equation

front: Sound passing through the interior of a liquid or gas travels only as a {{c1::longitudinal}} wave.
why: Sound only longitudinal in fluids; supporting detail for the wave-type card

front: Sound travels fastest in:
why: Sound fastest in solids, none in vacuum; common discrete

front: Wave speed on a string is $v = \sqrt{T/\mu}$, so tightening a string {{c1::raises}} its pitch.
why: String wave speed sqrt(T/mu) and pitch; beyond outline sound-speed basics

front: When a wave enters a new medium, what stays constant?
why: Frequency constant across media; foundational wave fact

front: A resting heart beats $90$ times per minute. What are the frequency and the period of one cardiac cycle?
why: Period-frequency conversion with a per-minute unit trap is common in physiology passages.

front: Angular frequency is {{c1::$\omega = 2\pi f$}}, measured in rad/s.
why: SHM notation shows up mainly as passage context.

front: Two identical pendulums swing side by side; whenever one is at its far-left turning point, the other is at its far-right. Their phase difference is {{c1::$180^\circ$ ($\pi$ rad)}}.
why: Phase difference is the basis of every interference question.

front: A mass oscillates on a spring. What happens to its period if the mass is quadrupled? If the spring is swapped for one four times stiffer?
why: SHM period formulas are secondary on the MCAT and appear mostly in passages.

front: The speed of sound in a medium is {{c1::$v = \sqrt{B/\rho}$}}, where $B$ is the bulk modulus (stiffness against compression) and $\rho$ the density.
why: The 'denser means faster' misconception is commonly tested.

front: A standing wave forms when:
why: Standing wave from counter-propagating waves; common discrete

front: For a string fixed at both ends, the allowed wavelengths are {{c1::$\lambda_n = 2L/n$}}.
why: String harmonics lambda_n=2L/n; standing-wave calculation every year

front: How do the harmonics of an open pipe differ from a pipe closed at one end?
why: Open vs closed pipe harmonics; tested every year

front: Two tuning forks at 440 Hz and 444 Hz sound together; the beat frequency is {{c1::4 Hz}}.
why: Beat frequency equals frequency difference; common discrete

front: What is resonance, and where does it matter physiologically?
why: Resonance definition with physiological examples; secondary

front: Two pulses meet on a rope: an upright pulse $3$ cm high and an inverted pulse $1$ cm deep. What is the displacement when they exactly overlap, and what happens afterward?
why: Signed superposition underlies all interference reasoning.

front: Two in-phase sources interfere constructively where the path difference is {{c1::a whole number of wavelengths}} and destructively where it is {{c2::an odd number of half-wavelengths}}.
why: Path-difference interference is commonly tested for both sound and light.

front: A tuner hears $4$ beats per second between a $440$ Hz tuning fork and a string. Tightening the string makes the beats slower. What was the string's frequency?
why: Beat-direction reasoning in tuning is a classic MCAT sound question.

front: In a standing wave, adjacent nodes are {{c1::$\lambda/2$}} apart, and a node and the next antinode are {{c2::$\lambda/4$}} apart.
why: Node spacing drives every standing-wave length calculation.

front: The first overtone is which harmonic for a string or open pipe, and which for a pipe closed at one end?
why: Overtone-versus-harmonic numbering is a frequent trap in pipe questions.

front: Described by pressure, an open end of a pipe is a pressure {{c1::node}} and a closed end is a pressure {{c2::antinode}}.
why: Pressure descriptions of pipes appear in passages; the formulas do not change.

front: A tube's two consecutive resonances are $150$ Hz and $250$ Hz. Is it open or closed at one end, and what is its fundamental?
why: Closed-pipe odd harmonics are tested on nearly every MCAT.

front: The ear canal acts as a pipe {{c1::closed at one end}} (sealed by the eardrum), so a $2.5$ cm canal resonates near $3400$ Hz.
why: A favorite physiology application of closed-pipe resonance.

front: Heavier damping makes a driven system's resonance {{c1::weaker and less sharp}}.
why: Damping appears qualitatively in resonance passages.
